bt67yj-k39706-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for section 4, announcing the topic: whether being everywhere is proper to God.

bt67yj-k39706-d1e113.summary: The paragraph answers affirmatively, without hesitation, the question of whether being everywhere is proper to God, citing Scripture (Psalm 138, Jeremiah 23, Wisdom 1, Job 11) and the Fathers, who argue from the Holy Spirit's omnipresence against the Arians that the Spirit is not a creature (Ambrose, Augustine, and others cited earlier when discussing the divinity of the Holy Spirit).
claims: Being everywhere is proper to God, as omnipresence and eternity together are properties Scripture and the Fathers ascribe uniquely to God.
The Fathers used the argument from the Holy Spirit's omnipresence to prove the Spirit is not a creature, against the Arians.
concepts: divine omnipresence as a proper attribute
anti-Arian argument from the Holy Spirit's omnipresence

bt67yj-k39706-d1e148.summary: The paragraph qualifies the claim: creatures such as the universe-as-one-body, the world by its parts, prime matter, or an angel (through an extended, divinely augmented operative power) could in some derivative sense be said to be 'everywhere' or in many places, but only God is everywhere primarily and through himself — primarily because he is wholly present in each and every place and part of place, and through himself because this is not owed to some contingent supposition (as with the angel, or as a soul would be everywhere if only one human existed). It quotes Aquinas (Summa I, q. 8, a. 4) that being everywhere belongs to God primarily and properly, since in whatever place is posited, God must be there according to his very self, not according to a part — a doctrine true according to the three modes already established (power, presence, essence).
claims: Creatures can be 'everywhere' or in many places only derivatively, by parts or by contingent extension of finite power, never primarily or through themselves.
God alone is everywhere primarily (wholly, in every place, not by parts) and through himself (not owing to any contingent supposition).
This is Aquinas's own formulation: being everywhere belongs to God properly and per se, since in any place posited, God must be there according to himself, not according to a part.
This doctrine holds true according to the three previously established modes: power, presence, and essence.

bt67yj-k39706-d1e202.summary: The paragraph draws the immediate consequence that, on the sense just given, omnipresence cannot be communicated to any creature.
claims: Being everywhere, in the sense established, cannot be communicated to any creature.

bt67yj-k39706-d1e211.summary: The paragraph extends the incommunicability claim to naturally eternal existence as well, since no creature under any hypothesis is everywhere, and on this basis condemns the error of certain contemporary heretics who taught that the body or flesh of Christ is everywhere (ubiquitarianism): though Christ's body is hypostatically united to the divine person, it is not itself God or a divine person but a creature (like Christ's soul), and so omnipresence cannot be attributed to it; further treatment is deferred to Book 4, distinction 10.
claims: No creature, under any hypothesis, is everywhere; hence omnipresence (like natural eternity) is incommunicable to creatures.
The ubiquitarian claim that Christ's body/flesh is everywhere is a heretical error, since the body, though hypostatically united to the divine person, remains a creature and not itself God.
concepts: hypostatic union does not divinize Christ's humanity

bt67yj-k39706-d1e240.summary: The paragraph addresses an apparent counterexample from Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechesis 14), who says angels are present everywhere: it clarifies this does not mean any single angel is omnipresent, but that God so employs the ministry of angels toward human beings that wherever people are, some angel or other is present, in the way one might say 'angels are everywhere present around us' without any one angel being ubiquitous.
claims: Cyril's statement that angels are 'everywhere present' does not attribute omnipresence to any individual angel, but means that God's providence ensures some angel is present wherever human beings are.

bt67yj-k39706-d1e264.summary: A closing bibliographic paragraph directing the reader to Aquinas's fuller treatment of this question in several places: on this distinction of the Sentences, in the Summa (the question and articles already cited), in the Quodlibetal Questions (XI, q.1, a.2), and in the Summa contra Gentiles (III.68 and IV.16–17).

bt67yj-k39706.summary: Capitulum 4 argues that being everywhere is proper to God alone: creatures may be said to be 'everywhere' only derivatively, by parts or contingent extension of finite power, whereas God alone is wholly and per se present in every place; this incommunicability rules out the ubiquitarian heresy regarding Christ's body and is reconciled with Cyril of Jerusalem's statement about the omnipresence of angels by reading it distributively rather than of any single angel.
claims: Omnipresence, properly understood (primary, whole, and per se presence in every place), belongs to God alone and cannot be communicated to any creature.
The ubiquitarian claim that Christ's body is everywhere is heretical, since the body remains a creature despite the hypostatic union.
Statements about angels being 'everywhere' refer distributively to God's providential deployment of angelic ministry, not to any single angel's omnipresence.
